issues.legal_issue: A challenge to permission for a limited-period tenancy is confined to whether the statutory jurisdictional facts existed when permission was granted.
material_facts: The tenant opposed recovery of possession after the agreed limited term, arguing that the landlord’s stated future need for the premises was not genuine and that the landlord had other accommodation available.
The landlord had obtained permission to create a written residential tenancy for a limited period.
issues.conclusion: The Controller may examine only whether the jurisdictional facts for granting permission existed at the time it was granted; an inquiry into the landlord’s bona fide need or other matters outside those facts is impermissible.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, the jurisdictional facts are that the landlord did not require the premises for a particular period and that the premises were to be let as a residence under a written agreement. Section 21 is a self-contained exception to section 14, which it expressly supersedes for recovery under that provision. The Court affirmed the analysis in S.B. Naronah v. Prem Kumari Khanna and applied V.S. Rahi v. Smt. Ram Chambeli, Smt. Dhanwanti v. D.D. Gupta, Inder Mohan Lal v. Ramesh Khanna, and S.K. Lata v. R.C. Chhiba.

predicates.limited_term_possession_proceeding: A landlord seeks recovery of premises after a tenancy created for a limited period.
predicates.permission_validity_challenged: The tenant challenges the validity of the permission for creating the limited-period tenancy.
predicates.challenge_based_on_bona_fide_need: The tenant relies on whether the landlord will genuinely need the premises as a ground to invalidate the permission.
predicates.challenge_based_on_other_non_jurisdictio: The tenant relies on a ground other than the absence of a jurisdictional fact existing when permission was granted.

issues.definition: When a tenant challenges permission in a proceeding to recover premises after a limited term, the inquiry remains confined to the initial jurisdictional facts even if the challenge relies on bona fide need or another non-jurisdictional ground.

issues.legal_issue: Permission for a limited-period tenancy is presumed valid and remains enforceable unless the tenant obtains a declaration of invalidity in proper proceedings.
material_facts: The landlord sought recovery of possession under the Controller’s earlier permission after the limited tenancy expired.
The tenant objected to recovery but did not prove the absence of a jurisdictional fact that would invalidate the permission.
issues.conclusion: The permission was presumed valid, and the tenant bore the burden of raising and establishing its invalidity; until declared invalid, it remained enforceable.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, and the principle, discussed in Wade’s Administrative Law, that an order remains effective for its ostensible purpose unless its invalidity is established in competent proceedings. It relied on S.B. Naronah v. Prem Kumari Khanna, V.S. Rahi v. Smt. Ram Chambeli, Inder Mohan Lal v. Ramesh Khanna, and J.R. Vohra v. India Export House (P) Ltd.

predicates.limited_term_possession_proceeding: A landlord seeks recovery of premises after a tenancy created for a limited period.
predicates.permission_granted: A competent authority previously permitted the creation of the limited-period tenancy.
predicates.tenant_contests_enforcement: The tenant objects to the landlord’s recovery of possession under the permission.

issues.definition: When recovery is sought under previously granted permission and the tenant contests enforcement, the permission remains enforceable unless its invalidity is declared.

issues.legal_issue: The Controller need not give the tenant notice of the landlord’s post-expiry application for recovery of possession.
material_facts: The tenant knew the limited tenancy’s duration and expiry date and knew that vacant possession had not been returned.
The tenant could raise an invalidity challenge during the tenancy and could also raise it if the tenant learned of the landlord’s recovery application.
issues.conclusion: The Controller is not required to serve notice on the tenant before issuing a warrant for possession, although an invalidity challenge raised by the tenant must be heard within the proper scope of inquiry.
issues.legal_principle: The Court followed J.R. Vohra v. India Export House (P) Ltd., holding that the tenant is expected to raise a challenge during the limited tenancy upon discovering facts that may vitiate the permission. If the tenant raises a challenge, the Controller must give both sides an opportunity to be heard; prior notice of the landlord’s recovery application is not required.

predicates.limited_term_possession_proceeding: A landlord seeks recovery of premises after a tenancy created for a limited period.
predicates.tenancy_expired: The agreed limited term has ended.
predicates.tenant_knew_expiry_and_non_vacation: The tenant knew when the limited term ended and knew that vacant possession had not been returned.

issues.definition: When the limited term has ended and the tenant knows that possession has not been returned, the landlord’s recovery application need not be preceded by notice to the tenant.

issues.legal_issue: A limited tenancy may be genuine when its duration is based on a reasonably certain future event and a reasonable estimate of when that event will occur.
material_facts: The landlord stated that the premises would be needed after the landlord’s son married, and the tenancy was limited to three years.
The son would still be about one year below the prescribed minimum marriage age when the term ended, but the marriage date could not be predicted precisely.
The tenant produced no material showing that the stated future need was a pretence.
issues.conclusion: The estimate of three years was not unreasonable merely because the son would not yet have reached the minimum marriage age at the end of the term; the stated future event supported a genuine limited tenancy in the absence of evidence of pretence.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958, a tenancy can be genuine when its term is linked to a foreseeable future event whose precise date cannot be predicted, provided the landlord’s estimate is not unreasonable and no other factor indicates pretence. The Court relied on S.B. Naronah v. Prem Kumari Khanna and its application in Smt. Dhanwanti v. D.D. Gupta.

rule.if: limited_term_tenancy and term_tied_to_reasonably_certain_future_event and estimate_of_event_timing_reasonable and not evidence_of_pretence

predicates.limited_term_tenancy: The parties create a tenancy for a specified limited term.
predicates.term_tied_to_reasonably_certain_future_e: The landlord links the limited term to a future event reasonably expected to occur.
predicates.estimate_of_event_timing_reasonable: The landlord’s estimate of when the future event will occur is reasonable even if its exact date cannot be predicted.
predicates.evidence_of_pretence: Evidence indicates that the stated future event or need is merely a pretence for circumventing tenant protections.

issues.definition: A limited term linked to a reasonably certain future event supports a genuine tenancy when the timing estimate is reasonable and there is no evidence of pretence.

issues.legal_issue: Additional evidence sought after the hearing has concluded may be refused when no cogent reason explains why it was not produced earlier.
material_facts: After arguments had concluded and judgment had been reserved, the tenant applied to introduce evidence that the premises had previously been let out.
The tenant had made no attempt to produce that evidence before the lower courts or before the hearing concluded in the Supreme Court.
No cogent ground for admitting the evidence at that late stage was shown.
issues.conclusion: The application to admit additional evidence was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied Order 41 Rule 27 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and found no cogent ground to admit evidence that had not been produced earlier despite the opportunity to do so.

rule.if: additional_evidence_application and application_after_hearing_concluded and evidence_could_have_been_produced_earlier and no_cogent_reason_for_delay

predicates.additional_evidence_application: A party applies to introduce evidence not previously placed before the court.
predicates.application_after_hearing_concluded: The application is made after the hearing has concluded.
predicates.evidence_could_have_been_produced_earlie: The party had an earlier opportunity to produce the evidence but did not do so.
predicates.no_cogent_reason_for_delay: The party provides no cogent explanation for failing to produce the evidence earlier.

issues.definition: An application made after the hearing to introduce evidence that could have been produced earlier is rejected when the delay has no cogent explanation.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord is entitled to restoration of possession when the limited tenancy has expired and the tenant fails to establish that the permission was invalid.
material_facts: The premises were let for residential use under a written agreement for a limited term with the Controller’s permission.
The tenant remained in possession after the term expired and objected to recovery.
The tenant did not prove that any jurisdictional fact necessary for the permission was absent.
issues.conclusion: The landlord’s application for recovery of possession was allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 21 of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 permits restoration of possession after expiry of a valid limited tenancy notwithstanding section 14 or other law. Because the tenant did not establish the absence of a jurisdictional fact, the permission remained enforceable. The Court applied S.B. Naronah v. Prem Kumari Khanna and the related authorities it discussed.

rule.if: limited_term_possession_proceeding and residential_written_limited_tenancy and tenancy_expired and tenant_failed_to_restore_possession and not jurisdictional_defect_proved

predicates.limited_term_possession_proceeding: A landlord seeks recovery of premises after a tenancy created for a limited period.
predicates.residential_written_limited_tenancy: The premises were let for residential use for a limited term under a written agreement.
predicates.tenancy_expired: The agreed limited term has ended.
predicates.tenant_failed_to_restore_possession: The tenant did not return vacant possession after the limited term ended.
predicates.jurisdictional_defect_proved: The tenant established that a required jurisdictional fact was absent when permission was granted.

issues.definition: When a written residential limited tenancy has expired, possession has not been returned, and the tenant has not proved a jurisdictional defect, the landlord is entitled to restoration of possession.
